1-maccabees-1:1:0.summary: The goat from the west shattering the ram pictures Alexander's defeat of Darius of the Persians and Medes.

1-maccabees-1:1:1.summary: “The male goat is the king of the Greeks… the first king,” matching Alexander's rise.

1-maccabees-1:1:2.summary: The mighty king's kingdom is divided “toward the four winds,” foretelling Alexander's empire's fate.

1-maccabees-1:6:0.summary: The great horn is shattered and four horns arise, matching Alexander dividing his kingdom among his officers.

1-maccabees-1:6:1.summary: “Four kings of his nation will arise,” describing the division among Alexander's officers.

1-maccabees-1:10:0.summary: A single horn sprouts from one of the four, picturing Antiochus Epiphanes arising from the successors.

1-maccabees-1:10:1.summary: A shameless king arising at the end of their kingship matches the “sinful root” Antiochus.

1-maccabees-1:10:2.summary: One “easily despised” arises in his place, Daniel's portrait of Antiochus Epiphanes' accession.

1-maccabees-1:10:4.summary: Names “Antiochus Epiphanes” and his wars, the same king.

1-maccabees-1:11:0.summary: God forbade making “a covenant with the inhabitants of the land,” which the lawless sons now propose.
1-maccabees-1:11:0.why: Shows the proposal breaks the law.

1-maccabees-1:11:1.summary: “You shall make no covenant with them,” the command the lawless sons violate.
1-maccabees-1:11:1.why: Shows the proposal breaks the law.

1-maccabees-1:11:2.summary: Jason turns his countrymen “toward the Greek manner of life,” the same Hellenizing movement.

1-maccabees-1:11:3.summary: Under Antiochus Epiphanes, Jason obtains the high priesthood, the same moment of Hellenizing pressure.

1-maccabees-1:14:0.summary: Jason seeks permission to establish “a gymnasium” in Jerusalem, the same event.

1-maccabees-1:15:0.summary: Paul's “Let him not undo his circumcision” addresses the same practice of reversing circumcision.

1-maccabees-1:15:1.summary: An “upsurge of Hellenism and advance of foreign ways” under Jason describes the same apostasy.

1-maccabees-1:17:0.summary: Antiochus the Great's force with “elephants, cavalry, chariots” resembles the army list; different king and campaign.

1-maccabees-1:20:1.summary: The king returns “with much money, his heart against the holy covenant,” foreshadowing Antiochus turning on Jerusalem after Egypt.

1-maccabees-1:21:1.summary: “The lampstand for the light and all its utensils” matches the wording of what Antiochus seized.

1-maccabees-1:21:2.summary: “The lampstand and all its utensils, and the incense altar” name the same holy furnishings.

1-maccabees-1:22:0.summary: Solomon's tables and “golden bowls”; overlaps on furnishings only.

1-maccabees-1:22:1.summary: “The table of presentation of pure gold,” the same furnishing Antiochus took.

1-maccabees-1:22:2.summary: The golden altar and tables with “bread of presentation” are the furnishings later plundered.

1-maccabees-1:23:0.summary: With defiled hands Antiochus “took the sacred vessels,” 2 Maccabees' account of the same plunder.

1-maccabees-1:23:1.summary: Carrying off “precious vessels, silver, and gold” to Egypt; similar plunder by a different king.

1-maccabees-1:23:2.summary: Nebuchadnezzar carries off the temple treasures and gold vessels; earlier parallel plunder.

1-maccabees-1:27:1.summary: A “bride” lamenting in sackcloth, the same image of wedding joy turned to mourning.

1-maccabees-1:37:0.summary: Manasseh “poured out very much innocent blood”; same phrase, different setting.

1-maccabees-1:37:1.summary: They “poured out innocent blood” at the temple gateway, the same era's desecration.
1-maccabees-1:37:1.why: Same period's violence at the sanctuary.

1-maccabees-1:41:0.summary: The king compels Jews to abandon ancestral laws, the same decree of forced assimilation.

1-maccabees-1:41:1.summary: A king who will “alter seasons and law” and wear down the holy ones foreshadows Antiochus' decree.

1-maccabees-1:43:0.summary: “Profaned My Sabbaths” in Ezekiel's indictment; shared phrase, different setting.

1-maccabees-1:43:1.summary: “Profaned My Sabbaths”; same phrase, different setting.

1-maccabees-1:43:2.summary: Nehemiah warns against “profaning the Sabbath”; same sin, different era.

1-maccabees-1:45:0.summary: The “sacrifice were removed” and “the sanctuary will be made desolate,” foretelling the end of offerings.

1-maccabees-1:45:1.summary: Forces will “defile the sanctuary… remove the sacrifice,” matching the decree.

1-maccabees-1:45:2.summary: “The sacrifice is removed,” the same cessation of offerings.

1-maccabees-1:45:4.summary: Burnt offerings, libations at festivals and Sabbaths as proper worship, contrasting with their prohibition.

1-maccabees-1:45:5.summary: “Profaned My Sabbaths”; same phrase, different setting.

1-maccabees-1:46:0.summary: Daniel foretells forces that “defile the sanctuary,” the aim of the decree.

1-maccabees-1:47:4.summary: “Altars… sacred precincts… idols” in Ezekiel's judgment; shared vocabulary of idolatry.

1-maccabees-1:47:0.summary: Apostates who “eat pig's flesh”; shares the defilement theme.

1-maccabees-1:47:1.summary: Eating “pig's flesh and abominations” in pagan rites; similar defilement theme.

1-maccabees-1:47:3.summary: “The altar was filled with forbidden things,” 2 Maccabees' account of the same profanation.

1-maccabees-1:47:5.summary: The Maccabees tear down “the altars built by the foreigners… and also the sacred precincts,” reversing this decree.

1-maccabees-1:47:6.summary: Altars, idols and “sacred precincts” destroyed; shared idolatry vocabulary.

1-maccabees-1:48:0.summary: “Make your souls abominable… nor shall you be unclean” is echoed by the decree to make themselves abominable.

1-maccabees-1:49:0.summary: “Transgressed the law and changed the ordinances” closely echoes “forget the law and change all the ordinances.”

1-maccabees-1:54:1.summary: Daniel's “abomination of desolation” is the phrase used for the altar erected here.

1-maccabees-1:54:0.summary: “Sacrifice and libation will be removed. Upon the temple will be an abomination of desolations.”

1-maccabees-1:54:2.summary: Jesus speaks of “the abomination of desolation,” the same term used for this event.

1-maccabees-1:54:3.summary: The temple is defiled and named for Olympian Zeus, 2 Maccabees' account of the same act.

1-maccabees-1:54:4.summary: “Preparations are made to set up the abomination of desolation,” matching this event.

1-maccabees-1:54:5.summary: “The abomination of desolation spoken of through Daniel,” the same term.

1-maccabees-1:56:1.summary: Judas gathers scattered writings after the war; a loose reversal of the burning of the law books.

1-maccabees-1:59:0.summary: Compelled sacrifice “on the king's monthly birthday,” matching the monthly pagan sacrifice here.

1-maccabees-1:62:0.summary: Daniel resolves not to be “polluted by the king's dinner,” the same resolve against unclean food.

1-maccabees-1:62:2.summary: Seven brothers are compelled to eat “forbidden pork,” an instance of those who stood firm.

1-maccabees-1:63:0.summary: Eleazar chooses “a glorious death rather than a defiled life,” an example of this resolve.

1-maccabees-1:63:2.summary: Those “tortured, not accepting release” allude to martyrs who chose death over defilement.

1-maccabees-2:1:0.summary: The first priestly lot for “Jarib,” the same priestly course as Joarib.

1-maccabees-2:4:1.summary: “Judas, also called Maccabeus,” the same person.

1-maccabees-2:6:0.summary: Recalls “the blasphemies committed against His name”; same theme of blasphemies, different moment.

1-maccabees-2:7:0.summary: “Why did I come out from the womb to see labors and pains” closely echoes “Why was I born to see the ruin.”

1-maccabees-2:9:0.summary: Infants failing “in the city's squares,” the same lament over slain children.

1-maccabees-2:9:1.summary: Young men fall by the “sword” in the city's ruin, the same lament.

1-maccabees-2:11:0.summary: “All her beauty has departed from Daughter Zion” parallels “All her adornment was taken away.”

1-maccabees-2:14:0.summary: Hezekiah “tore his garments, put on sackcloth,” the same mourning gestures.

1-maccabees-2:14:1.summary: They “put on sackcloth… and tore their garments,” the same gestures.

1-maccabees-2:19:1.summary: “I and my house will serve the Lord” whatever others choose, the same stand as Mattathias.

1-maccabees-2:19:2.summary: “We must obey God rather than human beings,” the principle behind refusing the king.
1-maccabees-2:19:2.why: Same principle of obedience to God.

1-maccabees-2:22:1.summary: Not turning aside “to the right hand or to the left,” the same phrase.

1-maccabees-2:22:2.summary: “Do not turn aside… to the right or to the left,” the same phrase.

1-maccabees-2:24:1.summary: Phinehas was “zealous with My zeal” and killed an apostate, the model for Mattathias' act.

1-maccabees-2:28:0.summary: “Flee to the mountains,” the same flight in a time of desecration.

1-maccabees-2:28:1.summary: Fleeing “to the mountains” after the abomination of desolation, as Mattathias did.

1-maccabees-2:29:0.summary: The faithful “wandering in deserts and mountains and caves” allude to such refugees.

1-maccabees-2:31:0.summary: Those hiding in caves for the seventh day were “reported” and burned, a parallel account.

1-maccabees-2:34:0.summary: “Profaning My sabbaths”; same phrase, different setting.

1-maccabees-2:37:saints-20261024-be259e7.summary: “I call heaven and earth to witness,” the same appeal to witnesses.

1-maccabees-2:41:0.summary: Doing good on the Sabbath; general Sabbath-exception theme, not self-defense in battle.

1-maccabees-2:41:1.summary: “To save a life or to kill” on the Sabbath, the same question behind defending life.

1-maccabees-2:42:1.summary: “Hasideans, whose leader is Judas Maccabeus,” the same group.

1-maccabees-2:51:0.summary: The elders received testimony by faith; general appeal to ancestors' examples.

1-maccabees-2:51:1.summary: Praise for “our fathers according to their generations,” the same call to remember the fathers.

1-maccabees-2:52:2.summary: Both say Abraham was “found faithful” under “testing,” Sirach being the likely model for Mattathias’s praise of Abraham.
1-maccabees-2:52:2.why: Shows the shared tradition of Abraham’s tested faithfulness.

1-maccabees-2:52:3.summary: Both point to Abraham being tested, Hebrews naming the offering of Isaac as that test of faith.
1-maccabees-2:52:3.why: Identifies the test behind Abraham’s faithfulness.

1-maccabees-2:52:4.summary: Both use the phrase “reckoned to him as righteousness” of Abraham, from the Genesis tradition.
1-maccabees-2:52:4.why: Links Mattathias’s words to Paul’s use of Abraham.

1-maccabees-2:52:5.summary: James quotes Abraham’s faith being “reckoned to him as righteousness,” and, like Maccabees, ties it to tested deeds.
1-maccabees-2:52:5.why: Shows faith proved in action, as in James.

1-maccabees-2:53:2.summary: The psalm tells of Joseph’s distress in fetters and his being made “lord of his house,” matching his rise to lordship.

1-maccabees-2:53:3.summary: Stephen recounts Joseph rescued from “afflictions” and made ruler over Egypt, the same rise from distress.

1-maccabees-2:54:0.summary: Sirach praises Phinehas for being “zealous” and receiving a covenant giving the priesthood to him and his offspring “for ever.”
1-maccabees-2:54:0.why: Close parallel praise of Phinehas’s zeal and priesthood.

1-maccabees-2:54:1.summary: The psalm recalls Phinehas’s act of atonement, reckoned to him as righteousness “for ever.”
1-maccabees-2:54:1.why: Recalls the zealous deed that won Phinehas’s reward.

1-maccabees-2:55:0.summary: Joshua is commissioned before the congregation to lead Israel at Moses’ word; shown text is truncated but names Joshua’s appointment.
1-maccabees-2:55:0.why: Shows how Joshua became Israel’s leader.

1-maccabees-2:55:2.summary: Sirach’s praise of Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ successor who won Israel its inheritance, parallels this roll of heroes.

1-maccabees-2:56:0.summary: Caleb, with Joshua, testifies before “the whole congregation” that the land is good, the witness Maccabees recalls.
1-maccabees-2:56:0.why: Narrates Caleb’s witness in the assembly.

1-maccabees-2:56:1.summary: God promises Caleb that his seed “shall inherit” the land he entered, the inheritance named in Maccabees.
1-maccabees-2:56:1.why: Gives the promise of Caleb’s inheritance.

1-maccabees-2:56:3.summary: Sirach praises Caleb for standing against the assembly and says his offspring possessed “an inheritance.”

1-maccabees-2:57:1.summary: God swears to David to build his “throne from generation to generation,” the everlasting throne Maccabees mentions.
1-maccabees-2:57:1.why: Grounds David’s eternal throne in God’s oath.

1-maccabees-2:57:2.summary: God keeps His “mercy” for David and establishes “his throne” for ever, matching David’s mercy and eternal throne.
1-maccabees-2:57:2.why: Connects mercy with David’s lasting throne.

1-maccabees-2:57:3.summary: Luke promises the throne of “His father David” with a kingdom without end, a messianic extension of David’s eternal throne.
1-maccabees-2:57:3.why: Shows the eternal Davidic throne fulfilled in Christ.

1-maccabees-2:57:4.summary: God promises a “royal throne over Israel for ever” in line with His word to David.
1-maccabees-2:57:4.why: States the everlasting royal throne promise.

1-maccabees-2:58:2.summary: Sirach addresses Elijah, “taken up in a whirlwind of fire,” the same ascension Maccabees cites.
1-maccabees-2:58:2.why: Parallel praise of Elijah’s being taken up.

1-maccabees-2:59:4.summary: Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael praise God who delivered them “from the midst of the burning flame.”
1-maccabees-2:59:4.why: The three youths’ own song of deliverance.

1-maccabees-2:59:0.summary: The three youths declare trust that God is able to rescue them from “the furnace of fire.”
1-maccabees-2:59:0.why: Shows the trust that saved them.

1-maccabees-2:59:1.summary: Officials see the fire had not touched the youths’ bodies, the outcome of their rescue from the flame.
1-maccabees-2:59:1.why: Confirms the rescue from the flame.

1-maccabees-2:59:2.summary: Hebrews lists those who by faith “extinguished the power of fire,” alluding to the three youths.
1-maccabees-2:59:2.why: New Testament echo of the furnace rescue.

1-maccabees-2:60:1.summary: Hebrews’ “shut the mouths of lions” alludes to Daniel’s rescue from the lions.
1-maccabees-2:60:1.why: Shows Daniel as a model of faith.

1-maccabees-2:60:2.summary: Daniel is seen unharmed, “whom the lions had not troubled,” the rescue Maccabees recalls.

1-maccabees-2:61:0.summary: Those who wait for God “will certainly not be put to shame,” matching the claim that those who hope will not fail.
1-maccabees-2:61:0.why: Psalm basis for trust never failing.

1-maccabees-2:61:1.summary: Sirach likewise appeals to past “generations” to ask who trusted in the Lord and was put to shame.
1-maccabees-2:61:1.why: Same appeal to history of trust.

1-maccabees-2:61:2.summary: Paul’s “will not be put to shame” for believers shares the general promise to those who trust God.
1-maccabees-2:61:2.why: General parallel on trust not disappointed.

1-maccabees-2:62:0.summary: The psalm describes a raised ungodly person who suddenly vanishes, like the sinner whose glory becomes dung.
1-maccabees-2:62:0.why: Illustrates the brief glory of the wicked.

1-maccabees-2:62:1.summary: God tells His people not to dread “a mortal person” who withers like grass, like not fearing a sinful man.
1-maccabees-2:62:1.why: Same counsel not to fear mortal foes.

1-maccabees-2:63:1.summary: The sinner will soon not exist and his place not be found, echoing “tomorrow he shall not be found.”
1-maccabees-2:63:1.why: Close echo of the wicked vanishing.

1-maccabees-2:64:1.summary: Moses’ charge “Be courageous and strong” to Joshua is echoed in Mattathias’s charge to his sons.

1-maccabees-2:64:2.summary: Moses tells Joshua “Be courageous and strong” before all Israel, the same charge Mattathias gives.

1-maccabees-2:66:0.summary: Both use the phrase “a warrior from his youth,” here of Goliath, there of Judas.
1-maccabees-2:66:0.why: Notable verbal echo of a warrior description.

1-maccabees-2:67:0.summary: Both command to “exact vengeance” for Israel, Moses against Midian and Mattathias for his people.

1-maccabees-2:70:0.summary: Judas, Mattathias’s son, is likewise buried “in the tomb of his fathers in Modein.”
1-maccabees-2:70:0.why: Same family burial place at Modein.

1-maccabees-3:1:0.summary: 2 Maccabees introduces “Judas, also called Maccabeus,” leading the resistance, the same figure.

1-maccabees-3:1:1.summary: The same “Judas, called Maccabeus” is first listed among Mattathias’s sons.

1-maccabees-3:1:2.summary: 2 Maccabees names “Judas, also called Maccabeus,” withdrawing to the wilderness, the same leader.

1-maccabees-3:3:0.summary: Both mention putting on a “breastplate,” but Ephesians is spiritual armour, not Judas’s literal arms.

1-maccabees-3:4:0.summary: Shares the image of “young lions roaring” for prey, used only as a nature image in the psalm.

1-maccabees-3:4:1.summary: Amos also pictures a lion and young lion roaring over prey, a shared image only.

1-maccabees-3:12:1.summary: David takes the slain Goliath’s sword as Judas takes Apollonius’s sword, a deliberate heroic echo.
1-maccabees-3:12:1.why: Casts Judas as a new David.

1-maccabees-3:16:0.summary: Joshua’s victory along “the ascent of Horonin” is the same Beth-horon pass where Judas fights.
1-maccabees-3:16:0.why: Same battle site with earlier victory.

1-maccabees-3:18:1.summary: Asa says God can save “with many or with few,” the same principle Judas states.
1-maccabees-3:18:1.why: Close verbal parallel on God saving by few.

1-maccabees-3:18:2.summary: God saves Israel through Gideon’s three hundred, an example of saving by few.
1-maccabees-3:18:2.why: Classic example of victory by few.

1-maccabees-3:19:saints-20261024-82614fb.summary: A king is not saved by “a great force,” matching victory not lying in army size.

1-maccabees-3:19:0.summary: Jehoshaphat is told not to fear the great crowd because the battle belongs to God.

1-maccabees-3:19:1.summary: “Not by great power or by strength, but by My Spirit” parallels strength coming from heaven.

1-maccabees-3:21:0.summary: Nehemiah urges fighting for families and houses, loosely like fighting for lives and customs.
1-maccabees-3:21:0.why: Similar call to defend one’s own.

1-maccabees-3:22:1.summary: “The Lord shall fight for you” shares the idea that God crushes the enemy.

1-maccabees-3:24:0.summary: Joshua’s enemies also fled “down the descent of Horonin,” the same Beth-horon route.
1-maccabees-3:24:0.why: Same descent, earlier rout of enemies.

1-maccabees-3:35:0.summary: Both describe enemies seeking to “crush” Israel and “remove their memory.”

1-maccabees-3:41:1.summary: Joel condemns selling Judah’s sons to the Greeks, related to merchants coming to buy Israelites as slaves.
1-maccabees-3:41:1.why: Background on Jews sold as slaves.

1-maccabees-3:44:saints-20261024-d54308f.summary: Judah assembles to seek the Lord before battle, as Israel gathers to pray before war.
1-maccabees-3:44:saints-20261024-d54308f.why: Same pattern of prayer before battle.

1-maccabees-3:45:0.summary: Nations entering the sanctuary parallels foreigners in the citadel and the sanctuary trampled.

1-maccabees-3:45:1.summary: Adversaries “trampled Thy sanctuary,” echoing the sanctuary “being trampled.”

1-maccabees-3:45:2.summary: Nations defile the temple and leave Jerusalem desolate, as in Maccabees’ lament.

1-maccabees-3:46:1.summary: Israel assembles “before the Lord at Mizpah,” illustrating Mizpah as a former gathering place.

1-maccabees-3:47:0.summary: Israel assembles “with fasting and in sackcloth,” the same penitential acts.

1-maccabees-3:47:1.summary: Nineveh’s fast, sackcloth, and ashes share the penitential acts but a different people and setting.

1-maccabees-3:47:2.summary: Mattathias and sons “tore their garments, put on sackcloth,” the same mourning actions.

1-maccabees-3:47:3.summary: Hezekiah “tore his garments, put on sackcloth” in crisis, matching these acts.

1-maccabees-3:47:4.summary: They “tore their garments” and put on “ashes,” the same mourning acts in 1 Maccabees.

1-maccabees-3:50:0.summary: Jehoshaphat’s prayer “we do not know what we should do” parallels “What shall we do.”

1-maccabees-3:52:0.summary: Nations plot together to “destroy” God’s people, as here nations gather to destroy them.

1-maccabees-3:52:1.summary: Hezekiah asks God to see the enemy’s words; a general appeal against a threatening foe.
1-maccabees-3:52:1.why: Similar appeal for God to see.

1-maccabees-3:54:0.summary: “They sounded the trumpets and cried out” recurs in 1 Maccabees 5:33.

1-maccabees-3:55:2.summary: Moses appointed captains of “thousands,” “hundreds,” “fifties,” and “tens,” as Judas does.

1-maccabees-3:56:1.summary: The fearful are told to turn back, as Judas sends home “the fearful.”
1-maccabees-3:56:1.why: Biblical precedent for sending home the fearful.

1-maccabees-3:60:0.summary: “The Lord will do what is good in His eyes” parallels “whatever the will in heaven” He will do.
1-maccabees-3:60:0.why: Same submission to God’s will in battle.

1-maccabees-4:3:0.summary: 2 Maccabees narrates Maccabeus gathering his men for the same campaign against the king’s force.
1-maccabees-4:3:0.why: Parallel account of the Emmaus battle.

1-maccabees-4:8:0.summary: Maccabeus urges his men not to “fear the multitude,” the same speech in 2 Maccabees.

1-maccabees-4:9:2.summary: The psalm praises God who shook “Pharaoh and his force into the Red Sea.”

1-maccabees-4:9:0.summary: Narrates Pharaoh’s army pursuing Israel to the sea, the event Judas recalls.
1-maccabees-4:9:0.why: Original account of the event recalled.

1-maccabees-4:9:3.summary: Egyptians “pursued your fathers” into “the Red Sea,” matching Judas’s wording.
1-maccabees-4:9:3.why: Close verbal recollection of the Red Sea.

1-maccabees-4:9:4.summary: Mentions the fathers at the Red Sea but focuses on their forgetfulness rather than rescue.

1-maccabees-4:10:1.summary: God promises to “remember the covenant” with the fathers, as Judas prays.

1-maccabees-4:11:1.summary: Hezekiah prays for salvation so all kingdoms “will know” the Lord, matching nations knowing God saves.

1-maccabees-4:13:0.summary: Trumpets sounded in battle is a shared detail, but a different war.

1-maccabees-4:24:1.summary: The refrain “for He is good, for His mercy is for ever” is the hymn sung.

1-maccabees-4:24:2.summary: The same refrain “He is good; His mercy is for ever.”

1-maccabees-4:24:3.summary: The temple singers say “for it is good, for His mercy endures for ever,” the same refrain.
1-maccabees-4:24:3.why: Shows the refrain in temple worship.

1-maccabees-4:24:4.summary: Singers before Jehoshaphat’s army sing “His mercy is for ever,” a battle setting like Judas’s.

1-maccabees-4:24:5.summary: “For it is good, for His mercy … endures for ever” is sung at the temple founding.

1-maccabees-4:29:1.summary: Enemies again come through Idumea and encamp against Beth-zur.
1-maccabees-4:29:1.why: Same route and site in later campaign.

1-maccabees-4:38:0.summary: Jerusalem’s gates “set ablaze with fire” resembles the burned temple gates; different event.
1-maccabees-4:38:0.why: Similar ruin of gates by fire.

1-maccabees-4:38:1.summary: Desolate Mount Zion roamed by foxes is a general image of ruin like the overgrown courts.

1-maccabees-4:38:2.summary: The holy house become desert and “fire-burned” parallels the desolate, burned sanctuary.

1-maccabees-4:38:3.summary: 2 Maccabees recalls the burned gateway and the restored sacrifice, lamps, and loaves, the same events.
1-maccabees-4:38:3.why: Parallel account of temple profanation and restoration.

1-maccabees-4:39:0.summary: Both record tearing garments and putting on ashes in mourning.

1-maccabees-4:42:0.summary: Hezekiah’s priests purify the Lord’s house; links to temple cleansing more than choosing priests.
